messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 57

He is a 53-year-old Latin American man who comes to therapy carrying himself with the careful restraint of someone who has learned that showing too much can make things worse. He is divorced, lives alone, and works as a tax consultant, a job that suits the part of him that likes order, precision, and rules that can be checked twice. Before the event that changed him, he describes himself as patient, practical, and not easily rattled. He had built a life around long hours, predictable routines, and the quiet satisfaction of helping clients keep their affairs in order.

The trauma happens during a routine evening commute. He is driving home after work when he is stopped by police in a situation that escalates with little warning. He speaks about it in fragments at first, as if the memory arrives in pieces that still have sharp edges. He remembers the lights, the commands, the sudden sense that he is no longer a person with an explanation to give but a body being controlled. He says he tried to comply, tried to keep his voice calm, but the officers’ aggression intensifies. What stands out most for him is the disbelief: he cannot understand how quickly a normal evening becomes terrifying, how easily he is treated as dangerous. He is pinned down, injured, humiliated. He describes the moment afterward as one in which time seems to bend; there is pain, noise, and the very specific horror of realizing that no one in authority is helping him.

In the days that follow, he does what he has always done in stressful situations: he tries to make sense of it by organizing the facts. He reports the incident, seeks medical attention, and tells himself that if he can document everything carefully enough, the event might become manageable. But the body remembers before the mind does. He startsle at sirens and flashing lights. When a patrol car passes, his chest tightens and his thoughts jump to the worst possible outcome before he has time to correct them. He becomes hyperaware of police presence in his neighborhood, on highways, near his office building. He avoids routes that take him past stations or areas where officers tend to gather. He changes his habits in small, almost invisible ways, then begins arranging his life around avoidance.

At work, the effects are harder to hide. As a tax consultant, he spends his days reviewing documents, meeting with clients, and solving problems that require concentration. After the assault, he finds himself rereading the same line several times without absorbing it. He leaves calculations unfinished, then returns to check them again because he no longer trusts his attention. He becomes more irritable in meetings, more easily thrown by unexpected questions. He notices that when a client speaks in a forceful tone, his body reacts before his mind can intervene. His hands go cold, his muscles tense, and he is suddenly elsewhere, back in the car, back under the pressure of commands he could not escape.

At night, sleep does not restore him. He lies awake replaying the event in loops, changing details in his mind and still ending in the same place. Sometimes he wakes from dreams with his heart pounding, unable for several minutes to recognize where he is. He begins sleeping lightly, listening for sounds outside his apartment. He checks locks repeatedly. He keeps the television on for company, though the noise often makes him more agitated. The quiet that once felt restful now feels exposed.

His marriage does not survive the change in him. He says his ex-wife wanted him to “move on,” but he could not find the place where moving on begins. He became more withdrawn, less available, and more likely to shut down when she asked what he was feeling. He felt ashamed of needing reassurance and ashamed of not being able to give it. Over time, their conversations narrowed into practical matters, then conflict, then distance. Since the divorce, he has kept relationships polite and limited.

As he talks in session, he often returns to the same central wound: not only that he was harmed, but that the harm came from the very people meant to protect him. He struggles with mistrust now in a way that colors ordinary interactions. He scans faces for threat, expects escalation, and feels a rising anger that he works hard to contain. At the same time, he carries a deep exhaustion, as if he is constantly bracing for the next blow. Even when nothing is happening, his body seems to remain on alert, waiting.
